subtopic: Moral disengagement: displacing and diffusing responsibility
passage: In the Class 4 lunch hall of the school in Darjeeling, the girls had a rule this week: nobody sits with Rinku. Dolma didn't start it. But when Rinku came towards their bench with her tiffin, Dolma moved her bag onto the empty space, like everyone else. Rinku stood there, then went and sat on the steps alone. Anirban sir had seen it from the corridor. After lunch he called Dolma to the staff room. 'Why did you put your bag there?' Dolma twisted her plait. 'Everyone was doing it, sir. It wasn't just me.' 'How many bags were on the bench?' 'Six.' 'And whose bag was on Rinku's place?' Dolma looked at her shoes. 'Mine.' 'So one of the six was you.' Her eyes filled. 'Tomorrow,' Anirban sir said, 'you can choose again.'

qa.q: How many bags were on the bench?
qa.a: There were six bags on the bench.

qa.q: Why did 'Everyone was doing it' make Dolma feel less responsible?
qa.a: When six children did the same thing, Dolma's part felt small and shared, as if no one person had really chosen to leave Rinku out.

qa.q: Which question from Anirban sir helped most, and why?
qa.a: 'Whose bag was on Rinku's place?' pointed Dolma to her own choice, so she could see that one of the six was her, not just 'everyone'.

qa.q: What was lunch like for Rinku?
qa.a: Rinku stood with her tiffin, found the bench blocked, and sat alone on the steps, likely feeling hurt and unwanted.

grounding: Shows a child who joins classmates in shutting a girl out at lunch and says everyone was doing it, until a teacher helps her see her own part.

subtopic: Moral disengagement: displacing and diffusing responsibility
passage: I'm Eshaan, Chinmay's older brother. Last Sunday I was on the balcony when the building kids picked cricket teams in the compound. Ravi from the second floor, the new boy, stood waiting. One of the big boys said, 'Not him,' and everyone turned their backs. Chinmay turned his back too. Ravi went upstairs. At dinner I asked Chinmay about it. He shrugged. 'Everyone did it. It wasn't my idea.' I said, 'But you did it too.' He said, 'If I didn't, they'd leave me out.' I don't know everything he felt. He didn't finish his rice. The next evening I saw Chinmay knock on the second-floor door with his bat. I don't know what he said. But Ravi came down with him.

qa.q: Who said 'Not him' about Ravi?
qa.a: One of the big boys said, 'Not him.'

qa.q: What might Chinmay have been worried about when he turned his back?
qa.a: Chinmay seemed worried that if he didn't go along, the group would leave him out too, so following everyone felt safer.

qa.q: What choice did Chinmay make the next evening, and why does it matter?
qa.a: Chinmay knocked on Ravi's door with his bat and brought him down, which showed he could make his own choice instead of hiding inside the group's.

qa.q: What was it like for Ravi, the new boy, when everyone turned their backs?
qa.a: Ravi was likely hurt and embarrassed, standing alone in a new building before going upstairs without a game.

grounding: Shows, through an older brother's eyes, a child who joins the group in shutting out a new boy and says everyone did it, then later makes his own choice.

subtopic: Moral disengagement: displacing and diffusing responsibility
passage:
Monday: At the science project table, the group decided Gurleen would not be in it. 'She's too slow,' someone said. Kishore didn't say anything. He just didn't pass her the chart paper when she reached for it.
Tuesday: Gurleen worked alone at the back. Ma'am asked Kishore's group why she wasn't with them. Kishore said, 'Everyone decided, Ma'am. Not me.' Ma'am asked, 'Did you pass her the chart paper?' Kishore went hot. 'No.'
Thursday: Kishore couldn't stop thinking about the chart paper. It had been in his hands, not everyone's. At the start of the period he carried a roll of it to Gurleen's desk. 'Our group needs someone to draw the diagram. You're good at diagrams.' Gurleen looked up, surprised, and took it.

qa.q: What did Kishore not pass to Gurleen on Monday?
qa.a: Kishore didn't pass her the chart paper.

qa.q: What was Kishore thinking about by Thursday?
qa.a: Kishore felt guilty, realising the chart paper had been in his own hands, so leaving Gurleen out wasn't only 'everyone's' doing.

qa.q: What was the turning point that led Kishore to act?
qa.a: Ma'am's question 'Did you pass her the chart paper?' made Kishore see his own action, and by Thursday he chose to invite Gurleen back to draw the diagram.

qa.q: How might Gurleen have felt working alone at the back on Tuesday?
qa.a: Gurleen likely felt left out and hurt, shut out of a group without anyone telling her why to her face.

grounding: Shows a child who helps exclude a classmate and says 'everyone decided', until a teacher's question helps him see and repair his own part.

subtopic: Moral disengagement: displacing and diffusing responsibility
passage:
Ojas, you said everyone in your class ignored the new boy, so it wasn't really you. Let me tell you about Bhola.
In Class 5 in Jabalpur, Bhola's father sold milk, and his shirt smelled of the cowshed. One morning a boy in the assembly line held his nose, and soon the whole line did. I held mine too. It felt like a game. For weeks nobody walked to school with Bhola.
When my Amma found out, I said, 'Everyone was doing it!'
She asked, 'Then how much of it was yours, Harish?'
I said, 'Only a little.'
'And Bhola,' she said, 'did he get only a little hurt?'
The next day I walked beside him. Two other boys followed.
So, Ojas, what part of today was yours?

qa.q: What did the boys in the assembly line do to Bhola that morning?
qa.a: One boy held his nose at Bhola, and soon the whole line did, Harish included.

qa.q: Why did holding the nose feel acceptable to young Harish at the time?
qa.a: Because the whole line was doing it, it felt like a game and only 'a little' Harish's fault; being one of many made the act feel shared and small.

qa.q: What was the turning point for young Harish, and what choice followed?
qa.a: Amma's question, whether Bhola got 'only a little hurt', was the turning point; the next day Harish chose to walk beside Bhola, and two other boys followed.

qa.q: How might Bhola have experienced those weeks, compared with how the boys saw them?
qa.a: To the boys it was a shared game with each doing only a little, but Bhola walked to school alone every day and carried the whole weight of it.

grounding: An elder recalls joining a whole line in shunning a classmate and claiming everyone was doing it, showing how a shared act feels like no one's fault.

subtopic: Moral disengagement: displacing and diffusing responsibility
passage:
Rain hammered the tin roof, so Class 6B was stuck inside for recess. Nikhita drew a chalk square on the floor: 'Secret club. Members only.' Eight girls squeezed in. When Mehak came over with her ludo board, Nikhita said, 'Full.' Then she looked at Disha. 'Right, Disha?'
Disha glanced at the others. Everyone was nodding. 'Full,' she repeated.
Mehak sat alone by the dripping window, lining up ludo pieces nobody would move.
Later, Ms Rao asked the club what had happened. 'I only said one word,' Disha said. 'Everyone else said it first.'
'Eight people, one word each,' Ms Rao said. 'How many words did Mehak hear?'
Disha counted on her fingers and stopped at eight. She looked over at the window.

qa.q: What did Mehak bring over to the chalk square?
qa.a: Mehak came over with her ludo board.

qa.q: Why did saying 'Full' feel small to Disha?
qa.a: Disha felt it was only one word and everyone else had said it first, so the blame seemed spread across the whole group rather than resting on her.

qa.q: When Disha looks over at the window, what choice could she make next?
qa.a: Disha could go and play ludo with Mehak or tell the club there is room; one person stepping out of the group can start to undo those eight words.

qa.q: What was recess like for Mehak by the dripping window?
qa.a: Mehak heard 'Full' from the whole group and spent recess alone lining up pieces; to her it felt like being turned away eight times, not once. 😔

grounding: A child who joins a group in shutting a classmate out says everyone else said it first, as if the shared act belonged to no one.
